turns.content: Hey. I need a gut check on something before I file it tomorrow morning. I just finished drafting a written counseling notice for Mateo, one of my cashiers. He was scheduled Wednesday 5–10 but called at 3:30 claiming he couldn't work because we scheduled him outside his availability. He saw the schedule Sunday and said nothing. I ended up solo-running register and prize counter during half-price Wednesday. The write-up cites failure to give timely notice under our 24-hour guideline. I'm second-guessing whether this is actually justified or if it's going to look petty. Can you look at the wording and tell me if it's sound?
Let me pull up your draft first.

Okay. Here's the draft text:

**Written Counseling Notice — Mateo R.**

*Date:* Friday, March 21
*Employee:* Mateo R., Cashier
*Reason:* Unscheduled absence / failure to follow notification procedures

On Wednesday, March 19, Mateo was scheduled 5:00 PM – 10:00 PM. At 3:30 PM, approximately 90 minutes before start, Mateo called and stated he could not work because he was scheduled outside his approved availability. Mateo viewed the schedule on Sunday, March 16, and did not notify management of the conflict until the call on Wednesday. This resulted in zero coverage for the position during a high-traffic evening.

Per store policy, employees are required to provide a minimum of 24 hours' notice for any absence or schedule conflict.

I'm filing it tomorrow unless you tell me it's going to blow up in my face.

It’s defensible **if** Mateo’s claimed availability was not actually approved or the schedule matched the availability on file. As written, though, there’s one pressure point that could make this look petty or unfair: you’re disciplining him for late notice while acknowledging that he believes management scheduled him outside approved availability.

Tighten the wording and separate the two issues:

1. **Availability conflict:** Verify what availability was officially on file and whether this shift fell outside it.
2. **Notification issue:** Assuming the shift was valid, he knew Sunday and waited until 90 minutes before Wednesday’s shift to report the problem.

Also avoid “unscheduled absence”—he did report it—and avoid “zero coverage” if you personally covered the work.

A cleaner version:

> **Written Counseling Notice — Mateo R.**  
>   
> **Date:** Friday, March 21  
> **Employee:** Mateo R., Cashier  
> **Subject:** Late notice of schedule conflict  
>   
> On Wednesday, March 19, Mateo was scheduled to work from 5:00 PM to 10:00 PM. At approximately 3:30 PM, Mateo notified management that he could not work the shift because he believed it fell outside his availability.  
>   
> Mateo stated that he had viewed the schedule on Sunday, March 16. Management did not receive notice of the conflict until approximately 90 minutes before the scheduled start time. As a result, management had to cover both register and prize-counter operations during a high-traffic business period.  
>   
> Store policy requires employees to provide at least 24 hours’ notice of an absence or known schedule conflict. Mateo is expected to review posted schedules promptly, notify management of any conflict as soon as it is identified, and provide at least 24 hours’ notice whenever possible. Future failure to follow the notification procedure may result in further corrective action.

Before filing, confirm:

- The shift did **not** conflict with availability officially approved before the schedule was posted.
- You have a policy requiring employees to review schedules and promptly report conflicts—not merely a general 24-hour absence rule.
- “Viewed the schedule Sunday” is something Mateo acknowledged or is supported by a scheduling-system timestamp.
- Similar late notices have been handled consistently with other employees.

If the shift genuinely violated an approved availability restriction, don’t issue this as written. Document the operational impact, correct the scheduling error, and separately coach him on raising conflicts promptly—without making the counseling depend on the 24-hour absence rule alone.

Yeah, that's fair. I'm going to pull Mateo's availability form from the file cabinet later tonight and see what it actually says. But I know what it says. I processed that form myself back in September.

Even so, pull the form. Your memory is probably right, but "probably" isn't a great foundation for a disciplinary document. Three things to check when you have it in hand:

1. **What the form actually restricts.** Does it say Wednesday evenings, or is it narrower/broader than you remember? If the form says, e.g., "no Wednesdays before 6 PM" and you scheduled him at 5, that's a genuinely awkward middle ground—technically outside availability, but only by an hour, and writing him up over it could look bad if he contests it.
2. **Whether anything superseded it.** Any later update, verbal agreement, or schedule change he might point to and say "we changed this months ago"? If there's ambiguity there, know about it before he raises it.
3. **The exact language.** If this ever gets appealed to your DM or HR, the form's wording is what matters, not your recollection of it.

One more angle worth considering: even if the form fully backs you up, Mateo's underlying complaint—"you scheduled me outside my availability"—may still land as sympathetic if there's any gray area. Your cleanest case is the notification failure, not the absence itself. Frame it that way and the availability dispute becomes background context rather than the thing you're litigating.

If the form contradicts what you remember, don't scrap the conversation—just downgrade it to a documented verbal coaching about reporting conflicts promptly.
Yeah, okay. I pulled the form. It's exactly what I remembered — approved in September, "cannot work Wednesday evenings." So Clara scheduled him right through it. That part's on us.

That changes the picture significantly. Clara scheduled him outside his documented availability, so disciplining him for not showing up to an invalid shift is going to be very hard to defend if he pushes back—and he should push back.

But the notification failure is still real and still coachable. He saw the schedule Sunday, knew there was a problem, and said nothing until 90 minutes before the shift. That's where your legitimate concern lives.

So the move here is to split this into two actions:

**For Mateo: a documented coaching conversation, not a written counseling.** Something like:

> **Coaching Conversation Record — Mateo R.**
>
> **Date:** March 21  
> **Topic:** Timely reporting of schedule conflicts
>
> Mateo was scheduled Wednesday, March 19, 5:00–10:00 PM, which fell outside his approved availability on file (no Wednesday evenings, approved September [year]). This scheduling error has been corrected with the scheduling manager. Mateo viewed the schedule Sunday, March 16, but did not notify management of the conflict until 3:30 PM on Wednesday, approximately 90 minutes before the shift.
>
> Discussed expectation: employees should review posted schedules promptly and notify management of any conflict as soon as it is identified, so coverage can be arranged. This was a coaching conversation, not a disciplinary action.

Notice what that version does:
- Owns the scheduling error explicitly
- Doesn't discipline him for missing an invalid shift
- Still documents the late-notice pattern in case it recurs
- Doesn't require the 24-hour policy to cover this situation (it arguably doesn't, since this was a scheduling error, not an absence)

**For Clara: a separate conversation about checking availability before publishing the schedule.** That's where the actual operational failure started.

If you file the original write-up as drafted, you're disciplining an employee for the downstream consequence of your own team's error. That's the version that blows up in your face. The coaching version gets you the behavior change you actually want without handing him a legitimate grievance.
Okay. I'm not filing that write-up. The coaching conversation record you wrote — that's the right move. I'll print it tonight and talk to him Saturday when he's in. Thanks.

Good call. One small thing for Saturday: open with the scheduling error being fixed before you get to the notification part. If the first thing he hears is "we messed up and Clara's correcting it," his guard drops and the coaching actually lands. If you lead with what he did wrong, he'll spend the whole conversation (fairly) stuck on the invalid shift.

And keep the Clara conversation separate and private—Mateo doesn't need to be in the middle of that one.

Good luck with it. If the conversation goes sideways or he disputes anything, come back and we'll figure out next steps.
